title: Group Chat Gremlin
pitch: Five friends choose a movie with a real Raft-style protocol: they elect a Planner, replicate everyone's ballots into a shared log, and decide once three ballots are committed. The visitor plays the network, holding, dropping or reordering messages and crashing one friend within a mischief budget, while ember timers go dark, elections split and the minutes of the meeting write themselves. A live panel of Raft's safety properties stays green whatever the visitor does, so the game is stalling them, steering which movie wins through ballot order, or discovering that agreement is not fairness.
whyNow: Timeless: group chats still struggle to settle on a film, and the idea turns a real, teachable algorithm into a game. It fills this week's owed wildcard slot with a playable simulation rather than another explainer.

research.summary: Prose analogies that cast Raft as friends choosing lunch or dinner are already common, and interactive Raft visualisations exist, so a passive explainer would be a repeat. What the research supports as new is playing the adversary. The FLP result (1985) shows that with fully asynchronous delivery even one faulty process leaves every deterministic consensus protocol with a possible endless run, the Two Generals' Problem shows confirmations cannot remove doubt over lossy channels, and Raft answers with terms, majority votes and randomised election timeouts that make split votes unlikely, not impossible. Raft's five published safety properties give a live monitor that stays green whatever the visitor does, while ballot order decides which movie wins, which separates agreement from fairness. Lamport's Paxos paper was itself an allegory about a Greek parliament, which licenses the comic tone.

facts.claim: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson result (Journal of the ACM, 1985) shows that every deterministic protocol for asynchronous consensus has a possible non-terminating run even if just one process may fail, because a crashed process looks the same as a slow one.

In Raft a follower that hears no heartbeat within a randomised timeout (150-300 ms is the commonly cited example) becomes a candidate for a new term; a majority of votes wins, each term has at most one leader, and a split vote simply triggers another round.
The Raft paper lists five safety properties that hold at all times: Election Safety, Leader Append-Only, Log Matching, Leader Completeness and State Machine Safety.
Over a channel that can lose messages, no finite exchange of confirmations lets two parties be certain they agree (the Two Generals' Problem); extra messages only move the doubt to the last one.
Lamport's Paxos paper, The Part-Time Parliament, frames the protocol as the legislators of an ancient Greek island and appeared in ACM Transactions on Computer Systems in 1998.

Casting Raft as friends choosing dinner or lunch is already an established explainer genre (a DEV Community post, a database vendor's film-themed blog post, a conference talk on what to eat for lunch), so the new angle is making the visitor the adversary instead of the spectator.
An interactive Raft visualisation called The Secret Lives of Data exists (reported by a third-party software listing; unconfirmed, one blended result).

design.coreLoop: The visitor picks a level (stall them for twelve seconds, make a chosen movie win, or run the unlimited-mischief sandbox), reads the five friends' ember timers and ballots, then holds, drops or reorders messages and crashes one friend within a mischief budget while the protocol reacts in real time or in single steps. Each run ends with the verdict, a green safety panel, a fairness readout comparing the result with the all-five-ballots winner, and auto-written minutes of the meeting that double as a shareable replay link.
sophisticationHooks: A deterministic Raft core (terms, randomised election timeouts, vote requests with a log up-to-date check, append consistency check, majority commit, step-down on higher terms) run as a seeded discrete-event simulation that can be rewound, replayed and shared.
A live monitor of Raft's five safety properties that no attack can turn red, so every level is about liveness and fairness, not about breaking agreement.

The verdict is a state machine over the first three committed ballots, so delay-based ordering changes the winner and shows that consensus is not fairness; a regret readout compares against the all-ballots winner.

A mischief slider from none to unlimited: at unlimited, an attentive gremlin can keep them re-electing forever, a hands-on echo of the FLP result, while bounded budgets and randomised timeouts are what let them finish.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built in one morning: a Raft-lite engine with an event queue, an invariant monitor and a fuzz test over thousands of seeded random attacks; an SVG ring of five friends with travelling envelopes, ember timers and per-friend log strips; five levels plus a sandbox and a date-seeded daily challenge; a minutes-of-the-meeting generator with persona lines and callbacks; a hash-encoded seed and action list for replay; keyboard play with pause and single-step; an about panel. Cut: log compaction, membership changes, more than five nodes, real networking, music.
risks: The simplified Raft has to stay correct under every gremlin action; a seeded fuzz run with the invariant checker gates the build.
Newcomers may be lost; level one runs hands-off with plain-English envelope labels and a hover glossary.
Prior art: dinner-themed Raft explainers and passive visualisations exist, so page copy has to lead with the adversary game, outcome steering and the mischief slider.
Real-time play has to stay accessible: pause, single-step, full keyboard control and a message-list view for reduced motion.

FLP and Raft statements on the page stay within the verified facts; the 150-300 ms figure is shown as a commonly cited example, not a rule, and the unlimited-mischief mode is labelled as in the spirit of FLP, not a proof.

Unverified: that a named interactive Raft visualisation exists comes from a third-party listing; the page names it only as 'as of 2026-10-11, per a software listing' or omits it. Friends and movie titles are invented; no real films, brands or people.
